newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Burma refugees vow to stay in Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: Burma refugees vow to stay in Bangladesh.

text.p: Hundreds of Burmese Moslems demonstrated in Bangladesh's Kutupalong refugee camp on Thursday, threatening violence and suicide to prevent being repatriated to their homeland.

"It's better to die here than in Burma where persecution is commonplace," said refugee Moqbul Ahmed who fled to Bangladesh years ago from Maungdaw, a small township in west Burma's Moslem-majority Arakan province.

"We don't want to go back to labour camps (in Burma), let our sisters and daughters be molested by soldiers and live a dreadful life," he told Reuters at Kutupalong, near the Burmese border in southeastern Bangladesh.
Hyatuz Zahan, a 55-year-old woman refugee, gave similar accounts. "Only a hell awaits us there," she said when asked if she would be willing to return.
"We will prevent any move to send us back. We will resist it by sacrificing our lives if necessary," she added.
Earlier on Thursday, Bangladesh postponed the repatriation of 200 Burmese refugees, known as Rohingyas, from Kutupalong following militant protests over alleged attempts to forcibly return them.
"We have cancelled today's repatriation of some 200 Rohingya Moslems as we don't want to inflame violence in the refugee camps," repatriation official Qamrul Huda said.
"We don't want to force anyone to go back," he told Reuters in Cox's Bazar, which borders Arakan province.
Other officials said the repatriation attempts were aborted after Rohingyas refusing to go back put on red headbands, carried sticks and knives, and chanted demands to stay in Bangladesh.
"It seemed to be too risky given the high-running tension," one official told Reuters.
Authorities had earlier stopped repatriation from the Nayapara camp after violence on Sunday left nearly 20 people injured, including six policemen.
It was not known when repatriation would resume.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Thursday some 21,000 Rohingyas in Bangladesh were refusing rations in a bid to win a formal pledge they would be allowed to stay.
Spokeswoman Pam O'Toole, citing reports from UNHCR representatives in the area, said the situation in the two camps housing the refugees remained tense despite Thursday's aborted repatriation.

"The refugees have put up notice boards saying they want the people sent back this week to be returned and declaring they will not go back to Burma until the military are no longer in power," she told Reuters in Geneva.
In two operations earlier in the week, a total of 399 of the Rohingyas, the last of nearly 250,000 who fled Burma in the early 1990s, were rounded up and sent back across the border.
The action sparked rioting in the camps and a protest on Wednesday from UNHCR Acting High Commissioner Sergio Vieira de Mello to the country's Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad.
O'Toole said the 8,000 Rohingyas in Kutupalong camp had now joined 13,000 more in Nayapara camp in refusing rations. "They are also refusing to send their children to feeding centres," she added.

Bangladesh foreign ministry officials in the capital Dhaka said on Wednesday the resistance by the remaining 21,000 against repatriation only began when news leaked that the U.N. agency was asking the government to let them stay.
"The refugees began resisting as soon as the information of the UNHCR proposal was leaked out to the camps. That is the crux of the problem," said one senior official.
The UNHCR argues that forcing refugees anywhere in the world to return home against their will runs against international humanitarian law.

Bangladesh authorities, faced with an unwanted burden on their already precarious economy, say most of the Rohingyas moved into the country in search of better living conditions rather than for political reasons.
Most of the original refugees have gone back under programmes supervised by the UNHCR, whose spokeswoman said on Thursday there had been no reply so far to de Mello's protest.
Van To Nguyen, UNHCR representative in Cox's Bazar district, temporary home to the Rohingyas, said Dhaka had taken the right decision by halting repatriation.
